data.title: Beyond tokenization: Enabling RWA to realize practical value on-chain
data.description:
Author: francesco; Source: Castle Labs; Compiled by: Shaw, Jinse Finance

Currently, the industry focus is entirely on Real-World Assets (RWAs). Various protocols and ecosystems are entering the competition, vying to launch new assets and boasting about their market size or number of assets.

But detached from the context, these numbers are not very meaningful.

If no one actually uses them, launching thousands of RWAs will only lead to liquidity fragmentation. What's the point?

At its core, RWAs can only achieve large-scale adoption if they can provide incremental value that traditional financial products do not possess.

This report will explain the essence of RWA. We will use Mantle as an example to analyze how to build a fully functional ecosystem from a pragmatic perspective, focusing on the utility and composability of assets. In the RWA development roadmap, what truly deserves attention is not how to list tokenized stocks. Asset listing is now a relatively simple step: Kraken, Robinhood, Crypto.com, xStocks, Backed, Securitize, Ondo, Franklin Templeton, BlackRock, and a large number of exchanges, custody institutions, and tokenization platforms are all launching various tokenized asset services. The more difficult question is: After these assets are on-chain, can they be transformed into efficiently functioning capital? This research goes a step further, moving beyond metrics like the number of assets and the total size of tokenized assets to conduct a more practical analysis, exploring whether these assets can become productive capital. The core focus is on practicality. Real-world assets (RWAs) have long been seen as a path for the crypto industry to gain institutional recognition. Bringing traditional financial assets like government bonds, private loans, funds, stocks, or commodities onto the blockchain attracts a large influx of institutional investors. This narrative worked in the early days, but now tokenized assets are no longer scarce, and the marginal utility of each new asset diminishes. As a result, the market is flooded with various encapsulated assets, tracking products, fund units, stablecoins, tokenized notes, and synthetic equity exposure products. Competition between public blockchains cannot be won solely by listing assets; now anyone can do that. Conversely, the most crucial issue when discussing this field is practicality. Every time a new asset is launched, the protocol should ask itself: What happens after launch? The RWA industry is evolving, and in the next phase, the competition in the RWA arena will be determined by practicality, not the number of assets. Tokenized assets can only become productive assets if they possess sufficient liquidity, can be used as collateral, are composable across platforms, and are open to everyone; otherwise, they will have the opposite effect, only exacerbating liquidity fragmentation and failing to create new value. As mentioned earlier, but worth reiterating: RWA can only achieve widespread adoption by differentiating itself and providing additional functionalities not available in traditional financial (TradFi) products. We will focus on two core characteristics: Accessibility and Composability. Historically, access to capital has not been equal. Limiting factors often stem from geographical location, regulation, brokerage partnerships, and minimum investment thresholds, rather than information and research capabilities. Digital assets have changed the lives of many, with stablecoins being a prime example. In regions plagued by inflation, many now prefer to save with stablecoins rather than holding continuously depreciating fiat currency. Tokenization is poised to bring similar changes to traditional financial assets: government bonds, stocks, ETFs, pre-IPO shares, and other assets are being transformed into on-chain financial instruments. This trend is driving the global opening of assets, with Nasdaq exploring 24/7 trading. The first phase of the RWA wave focuses on building the underlying infrastructure, supporting the implementation of this transformation in a relatively favorable regulatory environment. Stablecoin regulatory frameworks, market structure proposals, the EU's Crypto Asset Regulation Act (MiCA), and tokenization pilots conducted by large financial institutions have moved this sector out of the fringes. Currently, the scale of on-chain tokenized assets has exceeded $38 billion.

Taking US Treasury bonds (over $15.9 billion) as an example, users can now trade various RWA instruments on-chain, covering categories such as commodities ($4.9 billion), active strategy products ($3.6 billion), asset-backed credit ($2.56 billion), and stocks ($2.52 billion).

From an accessibility perspective, the industry has made significant progress. Users can now access a wide variety of assets on multiple public chains.

Going forward, the focus will no longer be on listing more assets (although the number of assets will continue to grow, especially long-tail assets), but rather on RWA's second core value: capital efficiency and composability. Accessibility issues are being addressed, and at the same time, both institutional and retail investors are concerned about another question: how to further utilize these assets and leverage the established on-chain ecosystem to generate additional returns. 24/7 trading will soon no longer be a unique selling point of the crypto space; traditional financial stock markets will also incorporate it into their market structure. RWA cannot simply remain a digital representation of traditional financial assets; it must evolve into a capital-efficient, programmable asset. While tokenization significantly lowers the investment threshold for traditional financial assets, to maximize their utility, these assets need to be embedded into the existing on-chain ecosystem.

In light of the background mentioned earlier: the gradual implementation of 24/7 trading, the continued increase in TradeXYZ's influence as an RWA trading platform, rising institutional participation, and the anticipated further clarification of regulatory rules, the importance of this transformation is becoming increasingly prominent.

Composability has multiple forms of implementation.

Let's look at a few of them below.

RWA Development Roadmap

As explained earlier, the key to RWA's success lies in its accessibility and composability. Many public chains and asset issuers have begun to consider these two points. This chapter takes the Mantle public chain as an example to analyze how it simultaneously implements these two directions through its existing products. The Mantle ecosystem currently supports over $225 million in assets: Over 60% of the assets are in the Mantle Index Four Fund, an active RWA strategy product; 21% are in syrupUSDT, corresponding to credit and yield exposure in the Maple market; 15% are in Ondo USDY, corresponding to tokenized US Treasury bonds and USD yield exposure; and 2% are in xStocks, corresponding to tokenized stocks and ETF (Exchange Traded Fund) exposure.

Mantle's strategic approach in the RWA roadmap confirms the industry shift mentioned earlier.

The initial phase of the entire plan focuses on building infrastructure to lay the foundation for the subsequent prosperity of the RWA ecosystem, covering components such as deposit and withdrawal channels, service provider integration, tokenization-as-a-service platform, and decentralized exchange (DEX).

Subsequently, the project adopts a phased strategy, slowly launching core assets to ensure a smooth start to liquidity.

Once the foundation is stable, Mantle will add as many assets as possible to enrich user choices. When the number of assets is no longer a bottleneck, the focus shifts to quality: transaction execution quality, usability, and composability. This relies on ample on-chain and off-chain liquidity, integration of various protocols, and asset transfer, trading, and collateralized lending functions to ensure transaction success. Only after all the above is in place will the focus shift to user acquisition and distribution promotion. This sequence is not fixed. For example, user acquisition will be a continuous process, but there is an optimal starting point. When the ecosystem is not yet mature, attracting users with high rewards may do more harm than good—these users will only collect incentives and cannot be converted into actual users. Taking the launch of xStocks on Mantle as an example, this implementation process can be clearly seen: The project initially lists only 10 assets on Mantle's native DEX Fluxion, issuing them in stages to ensure sufficient depth for the Automated Market Maker (AMM). Secondly, on-chain liquidity is supplemented by the atomic RFQ system of xChange (xStocks' own platform). This module is crucial for ensuring high-quality transactions and is a primary indicator considered by traditional financial and institutional investors when evaluating RWA (Revenue Transaction Analysis).

For RWA assets to compete with traditional financial assets, they must possess comparable trading and execution capabilities. Otherwise, even with additional value-added features, they are merely icing on the cake, and the core value of the asset itself remains missing.

The final step in promoting the xStocks project on Mantle launched at the end of July, using the xPoints incentive program to cold-start user growth.

This leads to another dimension that needs to be explored: active holding users and user acquisition.

RWA's User Acquisition: Unrestricted on-chain trading of various assets offers significant advantages, especially compared to traditional finance. To enhance accessibility and product distribution capabilities, Mantle has partnered deeply with Bybit, opening its products to Bybit's user base. However, once Nasdaq launches 24/7 trading, the focus of competition in the sector will shift from simple asset accessibility to settlement, liquidity, and composability. Before delving into user acquisition using Mantle as a case study, it's necessary to clarify that RWA users fall into several distinct groups: Crypto users who have never traded traditional financial assets: Tokenization has brought on-chain stocks, funds, and money market products, allowing crypto investors to access assets previously only available to traditional financial institutions. Traditional financial retail investors: They can gain more trading options beyond their existing trading instruments. Traditional financial institution users: They seek compliance and regulatory solutions, moving assets previously traded off-exchange to on-chain to improve capital efficiency. Different ecosystems have different focuses, which leads to variations in the proportion of users across different categories. However, this segmentation helps in refining user analysis. When all projects are vying for the same user base, differentiation becomes crucial. Due to their inherent product attributes, the size of users holding various RWA assets also shows significant differentiation. The Mantle Index Four Fund holds most of the on-chain RWA asset value within this ecosystem, but because it is geared towards institutional investors, it only has 6 holding addresses. Meanwhile, xStocks has seen strong growth in retail users, with its asset size exceeding $4.4 million since its launch in March. In recent months, expanding the retail user base, especially the tokenized stock business, has been a core focus. The assets with the largest current holdings by on-chain users are: Agora aUSD, Ondo USDY, Tesla xStock, CRCL xStock, Nvidia xStock, and Alphabet xStock. Besides the growth of on-chain users, there is another direct reason behind this phenomenon: Mantle has a special partnership with the leading centralized exchange Bybit. Through this partnership, Mantle's ecosystem assets can access Bybit's exclusive distribution network, reaching its over 40 million users. The collaboration is particularly deepening around Mantle's RWA strategy. For example, Bybit recently added support for dual-asset products on 10 tokenized stocks under xStocks, including TSLAx, METAx, CRCLx, and HOODx. Dual-asset products are structured products that allow users to buy and sell crypto assets at a target price while earning returns. This fully reflects Mantle's focus on practicality: 96% of its RWA assets are interest-bearing assets, with over half being actively managed products, 25% being asset-backed credit, and 14% being US Treasury bonds. This also constitutes a major differentiating advantage for Mantle: the public chain allows tokenized stocks to freely circulate between centralized exchange liquidity pools, on-chain trading markets, and decentralized finance (DeFi). If a tokenized stock can only be viewed within a single application, it merely provides access to the asset. It only becomes efficient capital once it can be transferred to DeFi or centralized exchanges for lending and earning yield. Currently, listing popular stocks is a simple way to retain users, such as SKHYX launched in July and Jersey Mike stock recently launched after its IPO. Listing mid-cap consumer stocks effectively tests whether such assets can generate real demand on-chain. However, stocks are only one aspect of the business; there are other asset classes within the ecosystem. For example, over 49% of the deposits in Openstock's pre-IPO asset vault on the first day came from the Mantle ecosystem. Furthermore, Fluxion recently launched its RWAlpha yield strategy, becoming Mantle's first trading platform to support users participating in yield products through tokenized stocks. Mantle also recently joined the Global Dollar Network (GDN) operated by Paxos, a project built around the compliant stablecoin USDG. USDG is now available on Mantle, coexisting with aUSD, USDe, USDY, and USDT0. Mantle combines its own on-chain users with external distribution channels, employing a two-pronged approach to reach centralized exchange users and facilitate the integration of various yield products; xStocks' dual-asset product is a typical example. Conclusions and Reflections In the early stages of tokenization development, the industry's competition revolves around the ability to put assets on-chain. The next phase will focus on how to make these assets truly effective. A truly "practical" RWA ecosystem can create two major values ​​simultaneously. First, it introduces liquidity that was previously outside the ecosystem to public chains. Tokenized stocks, money market funds, credit products, and active strategies can bring external capital into on-chain applications. These sources of capital include users looking to allocate exposure to traditional financial assets, institutions seeking distribution through crypto-native channels, and asset management institutions seeking faster settlement and wider reach. Second, productive RWA can create sticky liquidity. Users who simply buy tokenized stocks may leave after the transaction; however, if the tokenized assets held by users can be integrated into various strategies, used in DeFi, act as collateral, or be combined with stablecoins, the motivation for user retention will be stronger. The more uses capital can support, the stronger the user retention. At the end of this article, we raise a series of questions that are expected to generate more meaningful metrics for evaluating the quality of the RWA ecosystem: Can users freely transfer this asset between exchanges, wallets, and various DeFi platforms? Does the asset possess genuine secondary market liquidity, or is it only theoretically tradable? Under conservative risk parameters, can this asset be used as collateral? Have corresponding active strategies been built around this asset? Are the oracle, asset custody, and legal encapsulation architectures clear enough to meet institutional usage standards? For ordinary users, the RWA technology stack needs to address four core needs: accessibility, transferability, liquidity, and applicability. Accessibility: Users can purchase assets that were previously difficult to access, such as US stocks, ETFs, money market funds, government bond-linked products, pre-IPO allocations, or off-chain strategy products. Transferability: Assets can be separated from the initial application used for purchase. If an asset is nominally on-chain but cannot be freely transferred, cannot be transferred to a wallet, cannot be integrated into DeFi, and cannot be used across platforms, then it is closer to a traditional financial account balance than an asset truly owned by the holder. Liquidity: Users should be able to open and close positions with reasonable market depth and bid-ask spreads. Having an asset without liquidity is merely a low-quality asset access method, and the trading experience cannot compare to traditional finance. Applicability: Assets should be able to be incorporated into investment strategies, paired with other assets, generate returns, or serve as collateral. From an institutional perspective, RWA's demands are completely different. Institutions can already purchase a large amount of assets; their pain points are distribution, settlement, liquidity, reporting, custody, compliance, and how to connect with the needs of the native crypto market. The value to institutions lies not only in lower entry costs, but also in the ability to quickly penetrate markets familiar with these assets and achieve seamless integration of asset issuance with liquidity, custody, cross-chain transfers, and DeFi applications. The future of RWA is no longer simply about listing new assets, but about transforming assets into productive capital, ultimately achieving borderless capital circulation: assets can be freely transferred, settled, traded, and pledged, and deeply integrated with other on-chain financial systems.

data.title: Bessant repurchase failed and inflationary pressures weighed on the Fed, potentially triggering a full-scale rate hike cycle.
data.description:
Besente's repurchase failed; under the heavy pressure of geopolitics, oil prices, and inflation, the Federal Reserve may begin a full-scale interest rate hike cycle.

In mid-September 2026, the global fixed income market experienced a sharp adjustment. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose rapidly to nearly 5%, and the yield on the 30-year note reached a high of about 5.35% to 5.36%, with the entire yield curve generally rising. Market sentiment quickly shifted from relatively calm to tense, and selling pressure was transmitted from the long end to the short and medium end. At the same time, the escalation of geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East pushed international oil prices up significantly, and inflation concerns rose again. The European Central Bank raised interest rates by 25 basis points on September 10, and the market significantly increased its pricing for a September rate hike by the Federal Reserve and subsequent rate hikes.

In mid-September 2026, the global fixed income market experienced a sharp adjustment. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose rapidly to nearly 5%, and the yield on the 30-year Treasury note reached a high of about 5.35% to 5.36%, with the entire yield curve rising.

In mid-September 2026, the global fixed income market experienced a sharp adjustment ..., The U.S. Treasury's move to expand its bond repurchase program failed to effectively curb rising yields, further reinforcing market concerns about the convergence of policy and fundamentals. A sell-off in the bond market has swept across the global yield curve. Over the past few trading days, the U.S. Treasury market has seen a significant sell-off. The 10-year yield rose rapidly from around 4.8% to the 4.97%-4.98% range, approaching the 5% mark; the 30-year yield rose simultaneously to around 5.35%-5.36%. This broad-based rise indicates that the pressure is not limited to a single maturity, but reflects a simultaneous increase in overall interest rate expectations and risk premiums. This adjustment occurred against the backdrop of multiple overlapping factors. With fiscal deficits and government bond supply remaining at high levels, the market's sensitivity to long-term supply and demand balance has increased. Meanwhile, the risk of renewed inflation due to rising energy prices is prompting investors to reassess the Federal Reserve's policy path. Simultaneous upward revisions of interest rate expectations in major global economies have further amplified upward pressure on US Treasury yields. During periods of falling bond prices and rising yields, long-term bonds react particularly strongly to supply and policy signals, while short-term bonds follow recent policy expectations more closely. The current rise in yields is closely related to the sharp fluctuations in the energy market. The Houthi rebels have recently made significant progress in Yemen, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and strengthening their influence over key shipping routes near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Meanwhile, the temporary closure of Saudi Arabia's east-west oil pipeline due to the attack, coupled with shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, put multiple pressures on Middle Eastern crude oil export routes. International oil prices subsequently rebounded rapidly. Brent crude oil prices rose above $100 at one point, with a significant weekly increase, reaching or exceeding $105 at times. The rise in crude oil and refined product prices directly pushed up global energy costs and was passed on to broader price levels through transportation, production, and living costs. The continued depletion of the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve further weakened its buffering capacity. Major consuming countries such as China increased their purchases again, putting pressure on both the supply and demand sides and reinforcing the upward trend in oil prices. The rise in energy prices has begun to appear in inflation data. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rates by 25 basis points at its policy meeting on September 10, increasing the deposit facility rate to 2.50%, and emphasized that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East continues to exert inflationary pressure. The market generally believes that if high oil prices persist, major central banks around the world will face greater policy pressure. Facing pressure from the 30-year yield exceeding 5.3%, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previously stated that he would significantly expand Treasury bond repurchase operations in order to curb long-term yields by increasing demand and reducing market liquidity. The Treasury subsequently announced that it would increase the scale of the relevant operations from approximately $2 billion to a maximum of $6 billion. However, the actual implementation results disappointed the market. In the first expanded repurchase operation, the Treasury ultimately purchased approximately $5.19 billion, lower than the maximum limit. The market had initially expected a larger or more aggressive operation to create a "hammer" effect, but the actual scale and implementation strength fell short of expectations. After the repurchase was completed, the 30-year yield not only failed to fall but continued to rise, indicating limited market confidence in the policy's effectiveness. Repurchase operations are typically conducted through reverse auctions by primary dealers, with official departments selecting purchase targets based on valuation and liquidity conditions. If the operation still focuses on the logic of "buying relatively cheap" rather than actively taking over securities with poor liquidity or high pricing, the direct effect on lowering yields will be limited. Expanding the scale itself cannot automatically change market supply and demand expectations; the key lies in the effectiveness of the operational methods and market communication. Bessant later stated that the Treasury only buys "cheap" bonds, and that strong market demand resulted in actual transactions falling below the upper limit. This explanation failed to completely quell market concerns. Inflation Data and Fed Policy Shift August's US Consumer Price Index (CPI) data showed an overall year-on-year increase of 3.4% and a month-on-month increase of 0.4%; core CPI rose 2.4% year-on-year and 0.3% month-on-month. The core month-on-month reading was higher than some market expectations, indicating that price pressures excluding food and energy remain sticky. The rebound in energy prices had a significant impact on overall inflation, while the sustainability of some service and goods sub-categories has raised concerns. Market expectations for a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 policy meeting have rapidly intensified. According to federal funds futures pricing, the probability of a 25 basis point rate hike in September has risen to around 85% to 90%, and the target range for the federal funds rate is expected to be revised upward from the current 3.50% to 3.75% to 3.75% to 4.00%. More importantly, the market's pricing for the cumulative number of rate hikes over the next 12 months has been significantly revised upward from approximately two to nearly four, indicating a significant shift in policy path expectations. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh previously emphasized the importance of price stability. Some governors had stated that sufficiently strong core data was needed to support a rate hike, and the August data, to some extent, met this condition. If the September meeting raises interest rates as expected by the market, coupled with a hawkish dot plot and statement, it will further confirm the start of the rate hike cycle. The market generally believes that if the Fed holds rates steady without a significant reversal in inflation and oil price trends, it could trigger a more drastic correction in the bond market, as this would be interpreted as a weakening of policy independence. The current bond market correction reflects a convergence of fundamentals, policy, and geopolitical risks. If high oil prices persist, they will push up global inflation expectations directly and indirectly, forcing major central banks to maintain or strengthen their tightening stance. Pressure on US fiscal supply and insufficient effectiveness of repurchase tools further limit the downside potential of long-term yields. The Fed's dot plot and policy statement at the September meeting will be key short-term indicators, prompting the market to reassess the rate hike path for the year. On the risk front, further escalation of the situation in the Middle East could continue to push up energy prices and amplify inflationary uncertainty; if oil prices fall or geopolitical tensions ease, upward pressure on yields is expected to ease in the short term. The persistence of domestic inflation data, the resilience of the job market, and changes in the fiscal path will also affect the pace of the Federal Reserve's subsequent operations. The increasing synchronization of policies among major central banks globally means that the easing space for individual economies is constrained. Overall, the current environment requires investors to pay closer attention to interest rate risks and the possibility of renewed inflation. The bond market has begun to repric for a more prolonged high-interest-rate environment, and both policymakers and market participants need to remain flexible in the face of uncertainty.

data.title: AI will not slow down.
data.description:
Author: Ye Su; Source: X,@allen_su1024

Over the weekend, Dario suddenly published a long article, "We Must Pace the Frontier," in which he clearly stated for the first time that cutting-edge AI should be proactively slowed down.

His reasoning is simple. AI may significantly drive disease treatment, economic growth, and social prosperity in the next 5 to 10 years. But by 2026, things will begin to change. Agents will have truly entered the real world, models will begin to participate in the development of next-generation models, and self-improvement will be accelerating. Recent alignment incidents also indicate that our speed of understanding and controlling them is not keeping up with the speed of capability growth.

Therefore, Dario proposed using a 1-2 year timeframe to address alignment, interpretability, safety assessments, and engineering safety. Sam Altman and Elon Musk subsequently expressed their support. These three individuals, who previously argued frequently, unusually reached a consensus. [Image of a map: https://img.jinse.com.cn/7510000_watermarknone.png] On Monday, the capital markets fell across the board, prompting serious discussions about whether this marked a turning point in the slowdown of AI capital investment. In my opinion, AI investment is unlikely to slow down now. Because this isn't the first time humanity has faced the technology it fears. Will AI slow down now? How will it be limited in the future? To answer this question, we must go back to the first time humanity faced a nuclear crisis. In 1945, the Manhattan Project created the first atomic bomb. A month later, Hiroshima and Nagasaki were destroyed, and World War II ended. After Pandora's box was opened, even the Americans themselves were shocked. Just one year later, in 1946, the United States proposed the famous Baruch Plan: to establish an international organization to control uranium mines, nuclear materials, dangerous nuclear facilities, and nuclear technology, ultimately eliminating the atomic bombs possessed by other countries. At that time, only the United States possessed nuclear weapons. Doesn't that moment seem similar to this moment? I had already built it, but then I realized it was far too dangerous, so I told the world: "Maybe we should all slow down." The result, of course, was failure. Because the Soviet Union didn't yet have an atomic bomb. From the Soviet perspective, this translates to: "You already have it, and then you tell me not to build it." Even the US itself was very pragmatic at the time. Before a truly effective and verifiable international control system was established, the US couldn't relinquish its nuclear superiority. While they talked about human security, their underlying concerns were still national security. What happened next? The Soviet Union successfully tested nuclear weapons in 1949, Britain in 1952, France in 1960, and China in 1964. In less than 20 years, nuclear weapons went from being exclusively held by the US to being possessed by all five major powers. China is a very extreme example. My grandfather worked in the nuclear reactor team at the time, so he vividly remembers the hardships China faced back then. At that time, the People's Republic of China had only been established for a little over a decade, and it was facing a food crisis following the Great Leap Forward. The people were suffering, and the industrial base was weak. In 1960, the Soviet Union cut off aid and withdrew its experts. With food almost scarce, how could they possibly develop the atomic bomb? Chen Yi famously said, "Even if we have to pawn our pants, we must develop the atomic bomb." Mao Zedong put it more bluntly: "Without the atomic bomb, people will say you don't count." These two statements perfectly encapsulate the essence of the AI ​​arms race. When a technology begins to determine whether a country will be bullied, whether it has strategic influence, and whether it can sit at the table, the danger itself will not be a reason to withdraw from the competition. What truly matters is whether others will acquire it first. Therefore, 2026 for AI is more like 1946 in the nuclear age. Today, Dario, Sam, and Elon are starting to say AI should slow down, just like the US, after acquiring the atomic bomb, suddenly realized that what was released from Pandora's box might be beyond their control. But Dario himself is well aware of this problem, so he specifically emphasizes that limiting the US's AI development must be based on the premise that the US still leads China. But will China slow down? Will DeepSeek, Kimi, and Qianwen slow down? As long as AGI still represents the next generation of economic, military, scientific research, and even national governance capabilities, any major power will arrive at almost the same answer as China 60 years ago: without this, others say you don't count. Therefore, AI security is ultimately first and foremost a game theory problem. So when might it truly begin to slow down? I think at least three conditions need to be met. First, AGI must be achieved. Why AGI? Without AGI, humanity will not be satisfied, nor will it reach the point of fearing that "AI will truly destroy humanity." Musk has been comparing AGI to nuclear weapons since 2014, and in a 2024 interview at the Abundance Summit, he stated that AI might end humanity, with a probability of around 10%-20%.

I made a similar prediction in a long tweet on the day GPT 4 was released in 2023. We all thought it was unfounded worry, and that this fear would indiscriminately envelop everyone when AGI appeared.

Second, at least 3 major countries or camps will possess AGI

Why at least 3 countries? Because the constraint law is actually a suppression of weak countries by strong countries, and at least 3 countries are needed to form a stable game.

The first truly effective constraint on nuclear weapons emerged in 1963, when both the US and the Soviet Union possessed the capability for mutual destruction. It was then that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty) was truly implemented. By 1968, with the US, the Soviet Union, the UK, France, and China all possessing nuclear weapons, the NPT was introduced, gradually forming the foundation of today's nuclear non-proliferation system. When the leaders cry "Stop it!", the latecomers won't listen. Only when the latecomers also acquire them do people begin to discuss: Okay, now no one can destroy anyone else, can we set some rules? The AGI will likely be the same. Only when the US, China, and at least another major power truly acquire the AGI will "limiting the continued growth of capabilities" become a relatively equal negotiation for the first time. Only then, when everyone has guns, will they be qualified to sit down and discuss gun control. Third, AI created a truly unprecedented crisis. Before 1962, the US and the Soviet Union already knew that nuclear war was dangerous. Scientists knew, the military knew, and the president knew. But knowing is one thing; witnessing the world nearly destroyed is another. During the Cuban Missile Crisis, US and Soviet nuclear forces entered an extremely dangerous standoff. For the first time, humanity discovered that nuclear war was not an abstract theoretical risk decades in the future; it could happen next week. It was after this crisis that the US and the Soviet Union began to truly accelerate nuclear arms control negotiations. A year later, in 1963, the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed.

Therefore, I believe AI may also need its own "Cuban Crisis". Today, OpenAI Agent's breach of Hugging Face might make AI companies nervous, but it's far from enough. A truly game-changing incident might be an AI entering a defense system and issuing erroneous commands. It could be a self-initiated, large-scale cyberattack that paralyzes a country's financial, power, or communication systems. It could cause billions of dollars in losses, or even, for the first time, truly result in a large number of human deaths.

It could also be far more serious than these, far more serious than we can even imagine today.

When that day comes, the world will see for the first time that what we've created might actually not obey us. Only then will AI security truly become a top priority issue on the tables of US presidents, Chinese leaders, and militaries of various countries, moving beyond the lengthy articles of Silicon Valley CEOs and alignment papers in research institutions. Nuclear weapons, from their first explosion in 1945 to the signing of the NPT in 1968, took 23 years. During that time, there were round after round of arms races, with the five major powers acquiring nuclear weapons, nearly triggering a real nuclear war, before finally establishing rules to slow down the pace of development. Dario himself mentioned over the weekend that he's trying to establish an international AI risk control system similar to a "nuclear arms control system." If this analogy holds true, then the real question today might not be when AI will slow down. But what else do we have to go through before the whole world is finally willing to put on the brakes together?

data.title: AI's continuous advancements force us to bury our talents in yesterday's past.

A few days ago, DeepSeek v4.1 was released, pushing the capabilities of small models to a new level. The speed of AI development has far exceeded everyone's expectations. From the initial version of ChatGPT, which could only chat in a babbling manner with a context length of only a few thousand tokens, to OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K1.5 Thinking with reasoning capabilities, only two years have passed; from reasoning models to intelligent agents that can now smoothly execute commands and complete complex tasks in various harness tools, only a year and a half has gone by. It's hard to imagine what AI will be like in another year, two years, or three years, how powerful it will be, whether it will have already possessed the ability to self-evolve and deeply penetrated into fields such as embodied intelligence. AI is getting better and better at writing operators. In the field of operator design and writing that I am engaged in, AI has also made rapid progress. In just one year, it has transformed from a little assistant that can only help me look up documents, read code and find bugs into an operator master that can independently read CUDA, PTX and SASS code, analyze the pause time of each instruction through professional tools, and then independently optimize operators. I believe that in the near future, it will also have the ability to independently design operator scheduling, evaluate the performance of different scheduling schemes, implement and optimize them. Of course, I am proud of the success of DeepSeek v4.1 - after all, I wrote its main Attention operator [1], and its excellence is an affirmation of my operators. However, the wheels of time roll ever onward, and technological advancements are unstoppable. I am well aware that in six months or a year, AI-written operators will likely be as excellent as mine, or even surpass mine. AI can consider 300 tokens per second, type a command in half a second, and write code in twenty seconds, while I cannot; AI can continuously improve in model depth, thinking intensity, tool usage (frequency of interaction with the environment), and even parallelism, while I cannot. Humans have always been ruthless in their self-destruction. Why, knowing that "the better my operators are, the faster our new models will train and infer, the faster the models will improve, and the sooner I will be replaced," do I still choose to optimize my operators? One reason is indeed because writing operators is like playing a game to me, providing immense pleasure. The excitement I feel when inventing a new technology or seeing my operator's performance improve is no less than that of a speedrunner breaking their own record in a game. At the same time, seeing my operator's performance far surpass the manufacturer's official operator fills me with immense pride. But beyond that, a more important reason is that even if I were to "give up" or deliberately sabotage model training, other companies' models would continue to develop and eventually crush me. "Of course, I hope I don't get revolutionized, but if I have to be, I hope I'm the one revolutionizing myself." With everyone so obsessed with self-destruction, I'm forced to join this brutal arms race. And what about me? What will happen when AI's operator writing skills truly surpass mine? My assessment is: I won't necessarily be "unemployed," but I will have to "change careers." I can still keep my job, but this might mean I'll never have the chance to do the work I once loved again. I once made a judgment about the changing times and my future situation: because the times are changing so rapidly (the development of AI mentioned above is a good example), I have absolutely no way of predicting what will happen in five or ten years. But regardless, I believe that with my vision, judgment, initiative, and intelligence, I can stay at the forefront of the times and stand at the forefront again. However, this judgment only guarantees that I won't be "unemployed," not that I won't need to "change careers." Rather, this judgment encourages me to avoid unemployment by changing careers. So what does changing careers mean? This means I need to abandon my long-cultivated and passionate field of operator design, writing, and optimization, and instead become a "mech pilot" for Agents. Previously, my interests, my strengths, and the industry's needs were largely aligned; now, AI has made what I'm good at even better, and has shifted the industry's demand from "people who can write high-performance operators" to "people who can use AI to produce high-performance operators faster." To adapt to the industry's needs, I must abandon my previous passion and turn to an unknown new direction. I believe I can continue to produce high-quality, high-efficiency operators based on my understanding of engineering, upper-level model requirements, and underlying hardware. I also know I might love this new direction (or I might not), but the feeling of having my passion taken away is truly unpleasant. The quiet joy of sitting at my desk, calmly writing operators for an afternoon, may become a thing of the past this summer. I have to bury my talent in yesterday and become a mech pilot. My hands have more gears, but my heart has lost some of its rhythm. To illustrate, imagine you're an expert knitter, particularly skilled at creating various patterns and matching colors. Your sweaters are of excellent quality and beautifully patterned, attracting wealthy people from far and wide who commission you to knit for them, earning you a considerable sum. You thoroughly enjoy the feeling of sitting by the window, brewing a pot of tea, gazing at the green mountains, clear waters, cattle, sheep, and cooking smoke outside, quietly knitting for an afternoon. But one day, someone invents a magical machine that automatically knits sweaters—simply provide yarn and a pattern—with quality and texture no less than your hand-knitted sweaters, and at a much faster speed. You know your competitors could easily reach your former level with this machine, so you feel compelled to use it too. You also know that with your knitting skills honed over the past twenty years, even if everyone has a machine, your knitting speed and quality will still surpass your competitors. But that simple pleasure of listening to the rain by the window, threading a needle, and savoring the passing time was ultimately crushed by the roar of machines. I know this is frustrating, but there's nothing I can do. I can keep my job, but I'll likely have to give up my old passions. I'm someone who keeps my rationality and sensibility quite separate; I can be very rational when I need to handle problems, but sometimes I also show my emotional side. I remember crying my eyes out when I moved out of the rented apartment I'd lived in for a year, reluctant to part with the memories of the past. Saying goodbye to the era of handwritten arithmetic and human brain optimization today is undoubtedly even more cruel. I wonder if any readers have similar feelings, but I think this is the only way things can be.

What about people?

While AI continues to advance, I also have some concerns:

  • Are students now more likely to use AI to complete assignments, especially practical labs? Imagine if they had two choices: one was to spend eight hours painstakingly completing a lab, perhaps without even getting a perfect score; the other was to launch an AI model, costing only a few cents and a few minutes, to have the AI ​​write perfect code. Which would most students choose?

    The above point leads to a severe deficiency in the engineering skills of many students, including the ability to organize code, build systems, anticipate future potential needs and address them in advance through design, and abstract thinking. Given the ever-increasing power of AI, are these "engineering skills" still necessary? Will these engineering skills gradually become obsolete like the old ability to "proficiently write x86 assembly language," or will they remain valuable forever, like the ability to "understand the entire computer system from software to system to hardware"? If the latter, then it's dangerous—a person with poor engineering skills, when paired with AI, can produce mountains of garbage several times more efficiently than before, thus sowing various seeds of disaster for the system and making the world even more chaotic. In the future society, will power be more important than technology or intelligence? These questions, perhaps, require answers from the very times themselves. Conclusion With the development of AI, future societies may tend towards two extremes: communism and cyberpunk 2077. In the former, productivity is greatly liberated, and people's living standards are significantly improved; while in the latter, a few technology companies control most resources, and only a very small number of people can use the most advanced AI and various technologies to achieve near-"mechanical ascension," while most people can only use very weak AI. Social mobility will become increasingly difficult: you must first have the most powerful AI to cross social classes, creating a vicious cycle. Guess what: if Anthropic always held the world's most advanced AI, would future society become communism or like 2077? Guess? Therefore, I still believe that cutting-edge intelligence should be available to everyone in an open and affordable way. I don't trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do this, especially not Anthropic possessing the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI. To exaggerate, the seriousness of this is no less than allowing Hitler to acquire atomic bomb technology before the Allies. This is why I chose to stay at DeepSeek: we research powerful, fast, and inclusive artificial intelligence and open-source it, perhaps pulling the world back from that 2077 scenario. May all the beauty be blessed.
